title: Choosing what to replicate
objectives: Decide exactly which numbers you will reproduce.

screens.title: Sort the targets
screens.prose: Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers" (JT), report more than one result. Before any code, decide what you will reproduce and how closely. Our data is the seeded panel.

state.caption: Our data: the seeded panel. It plants continuation and reversal, but no calendar effect.

screens.question: Put each target where it belongs.

slots.label: Out of reach with our data

hints.text: For each target, ask: does the paper give a quotable number, a direction, or something our panel lacks?
Only two cells come with numbers we can quote.
6/6 and 12/3 match the number; grid, skip and reversal match the pattern; January is out of reach.

feedback.correct: Correct. Two numbers, three patterns, one out of reach.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the right-hand column: a number, a direction, or a feature our panel lacks.

byKey.t6: Our generator plants no calendar effect, so January is like any other month. It is out of reach with our data.
byKey.t3: We can quote only two of the paper's sixteen cells. The grid can match in pattern, not cell by cell.
byKey.t4: What we can quote is a direction: every cell rises a little. Match that sign.
byKey.t5: The reversal is a shape over years, with no figure we can quote. Match its sign.
byKey.t1: We can quote this cell's number, about 0.95%, so we can compare numbers.
byKey.t2: We can quote this cell's number, about 1.31%, so we can compare numbers.

explain.text: Targets with a quotable number are compared number to number. Targets the paper describes in words are matched in sign and pattern. January needs seasonality our panel does not plant, so we say so instead of faking it.

screens.title: How close is close
screens.prose: A colleague replicates the 6/6 cell on free data and gets 0.41% a month, standard error 0.30%. The paper reports about 0.95%. The band is the paper's number plus or minus k standard errors.
screens.question: What is the smallest k on the slider that puts 0.41% inside the band?

hints.text: Slide k up until the band reaches the colleague's point.
0.54 / 0.30 = 1.8 standard errors, so k = 2 is the first stop that covers it.

feedback.correct: Correct. At k = 2 the band starts at 0.35%.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find where the band's left end passes 0.41.

byKey.onehalf: At k = 1.5 the band starts at 0.50%, still above 0.41%.
byKey.one: At k = 1 the band starts at 0.65%, well above 0.41%.

explain.text: The colleague is 0.54 / 0.30 = 1.8 standard errors below the paper. A rule of k = 2 calls that a match; k = 1 does not. So the rule must be fixed before the result is seen.

screens.title: What matching means
screens.prose: A replication rarely gets the paper's digits. We call a cell a **match** when it agrees in the ways that matter. The rule you just used is one of them.
screens.question: Which belong in the definition of a match? Select all that apply.

options.text: The same sign as the paper's cell
Within a stated number of standard errors
The same pattern across cells, such as rising in J
Any remaining gap has a cause you can name
Every digit equal
options.why: Sampling noise alone moves the second decimal. Asking for every digit fails every honest replication.

options.text: Larger than the paper's number
options.why: You treated a bigger number as better. A match is about agreement, not size.

hints.text: Would an honest replication on different data get every digit?
Sign, distance in standard errors, pattern and an explained gap are all testable.
Four statements. Leave out every digit equal and larger.

feedback.correct: Correct. Sign, size within k standard errors, pattern, and an explained gap.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep what an honest replication on new data could achieve.

explain.text: A match agrees in sign, in size within k standard errors, and in pattern across cells. Any gap left needs a named cause, such as a different universe. Equal digits are not a goal, because noise moves them.

screens.title: Apply the rule
screens.prose: The colleague now has two cells. Use k = 2: a cell matches when the gap is at most two standard errors.

state.caption: % a month. The colleague's numbers are made up for this screen.

screens.question: Fill in each gap in standard errors, to 2 decimal places, and whether it matches.

hints.text: Gap in standard errors = |colleague − paper| / standard error.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide each gap by its own standard error, then compare with 2.

explain.text: 6/6 is 1.10 standard errors from the paper, inside the rule. 12/3 is 2.39 away, outside it. The note reports both, and the 12/3 gap becomes something to explain.

screens.title: A cell that disagrees with itself
screens.prose: Sometimes the paper is the problem. This made-up row prints Sell, Buy and Buy − Sell for one cell. Rounding moves a spread by 0.01 at most.

state.caption: A made-up table row, % a month.

screens.question: What should Buy − Sell be, in % a month?

hints.text: Recompute the spread from the two legs.

feedback.correct: Correct. 0.51, so the printed 0.59 is a misprint or a different sample.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the Sell row from the Buy row.

byKey.printed: You copied the printed spread. Recompute it: 1.71 − 1.20 = 0.51.
byKey.sum: You added the legs. Buy − Sell subtracts them.

explain.text: The legs give 0.51, which rounding cannot turn into 0.59. Either a digit is wrong or the cell uses a different sample length. Record both numbers and compare yours with each, saying which you trust.

screens.title: The best cell
screens.prose: A colleague computes all sixteen cells on our panel. Then she writes: "Replicated JT: 1.31% a month, t 3.18." That is the 12/3 cell.

state.caption: Our seeded panel, Buy − Sell, % a month.

screens.question: What is wrong with the claim?

options.text: The cell was chosen after seeing all sixteen, so its t overstates the evidence
Nothing: 12/3 is the paper's best cell too
options.why: You treated a pick made after seeing the results as a target stated before. Choosing the best of sixteen inflates it, whatever the paper found.

options.text: The t statistic is too low to report
options.why: A t of 3.18 is not low. The problem is how the cell was chosen.

options.text: It should report the smallest cell instead
options.why: Picking the worst cell after the fact is just as much a choice made on the results.

hints.text: When was 12/3 chosen, before or after the table existed?
Sixteen tries give sixteen chances to look good.
State the targets first. Here they are 6/6 and 12/3, chosen because the paper quotes them.

feedback.correct: Correct. Choosing after looking is data snooping.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask when, and why, that cell was chosen.

byKey.fine: You treated a pick made after seeing the results as a target stated before. Choosing the best of sixteen inflates it, whatever the paper found.

explain.text: The best of sixteen noisy cells looks better than any one cell would, as the testing course showed. Our targets were fixed earlier, from what the paper quotes. Then the 12/3 match counts, and the other fourteen cells are reported as a pattern.

screens.title: The tolerance rule
screens.prose: Fix $k$ before you compute. Let $s$ be the sd of our monthly spreads and $n$ the number of months. Then a cell is a match when $$|\hat\mu_{\text{ours}} - \mu_{\text{paper}}| \le k \cdot \text{se}, \qquad \text{se} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.$$
screens.question: With se 0.35% and k = 2, which gap fails the rule?

options.why: One standard error is well inside a two standard error rule.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each gap with 2 × 0.35% = 0.70%.

explain.text: The rule allows 2 × 0.35% = 0.70%. Only the 0.80% gap is outside it. With 289 months and sd 5.98%, our 6/6 standard error is about 0.35%.

screens.title: The rule in code
screens.prose: Write the rule for one cell, then the share of the paper's reported cells that match. Tables are dicts keyed by `(J, K)`. Our table has more cells than the paper quotes.

state.caption: % a month. The colleague's numbers are made up for this screen.

screens.question: Complete `within_tolerance(ours, theirs, se, k=2)` and `matches(table_ours, table_theirs, se_table, k=2)`.

widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests, including a gap exactly on the boundary, which counts as a match.

hints.text: A match is |ours − theirs| ≤ k × se.
Loop over the paper's cells only, and look each one up in the other two tables.
`return abs(ours - theirs) <= k * se`, and inside the loop `if within_tolerance(table_ours[cell], table_theirs[cell], se_table[cell], k): hits += 1`.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the ≤ on the boundary and that the loop counts only the paper's cells.

explain.text: The colleague matches at 6/6 but not 12/3. So the share is 0.5 at k = 2 and 0 at k = 1. A gap exactly on the boundary counts, because the rule says at most.

screens.question: Which one-line answer is honest and complete?

options.text: 6/6 and 12/3 within two standard errors on a seeded panel; three more in pattern; January out of reach
The paper
options.why: That claims every table in it. Name the cells, the rule and the data.

options.text: All sixteen cells, within rounding
options.why: We can quote only two of the paper's cells, so sixteen cannot be checked.

options.text: Momentum, with a t of 3.18
options.why: That is the best cell, picked after seeing all sixteen, and it hides the data.

hints.text: A good answer names the targets, the rule and the data.
The targets were 6/6 and 12/3 by number, three by pattern, one out of reach.
The first answer names all three: cells, rule and data.

feedback.correct: Correct. Targets, rule and data in one line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the answer that says what, how closely, and on what.

explain.text: The honest line names what was matched, by which rule, on which data. It also says what was out of reach, so nobody reads more into it. That sentence opens the replication note.

ideas: Sort targets before computing: match the number, match sign and pattern, or out of reach.
A cell matches when $|\text{ours} - \text{paper}| \le k \cdot \text{se}$, with k fixed in advance.
State the targets before you see your table, so the best cell cannot choose itself.

formula.name: The tolerance rule
formula.note: k is chosen before the results, often 2.

summary.trap: Choosing the best-looking cell after computing all sixteen, then calling it the replication.

quiz.prose: Our cell is 0.50% a month from the paper's, with standard error 0.20%. The rule is k = 2.
quiz.question: Is it a match?

options.text: No: the gap is 2.5 standard errors
Yes: 0.50% is a small gap
options.why: You judged the gap by eye. Measured in standard errors it is 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5, beyond 2.

options.text: Yes: the gap is 0.4 standard errors
options.why: You divided the standard error by the gap. It is 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gap by the standard error.

explain.text: 0.50 / 0.20 = 2.5 standard errors, more than the 2 the rule allows. The gap goes in the note with a likely cause.

quiz.prose: A spread series has sd 6.0% a month over 289 months.
quiz.question: What is the standard error of its mean, in % a month?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the sd by √n.

byKey.sd: That is the sd itself. The standard error divides it by √289 = 17.
byKey.n: You divided by n. The standard error divides by √n.

explain.text: √289 = 17, so the standard error is 6.0 / 17 = 0.353% a month. A two standard error rule allows about 0.71%.

quiz.prose: The paper reports that the losers' returns are concentrated in January.
quiz.question: Why can our seeded panel not reproduce this?

options.text: The generator plants no calendar effect, so January is like any other month
The panel is too short
options.why: Our 300 months hold 25 Januaries. Length is not the problem.

options.text: The panel is too noisy
options.why: Noise would blur an effect, not remove one the generator never plants.

options.text: The panel has no losers
options.why: Every month has a bottom decile. What is missing is seasonality.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the generator puts in.

explain.text: A seeded panel contains only what we plant: continuation, reversal, factors and noise. Nothing depends on the month of the year. So the January result is listed as out of reach, not tested.
